div.head: The design of hard real time systems involves complex issues because requirements of time, pe$ormance and security must be met. Many authors have developed methods in order to assure delays are bounded in the system, but there is not so much work that assures bounding delays in distributed real time systems over industrial fieldbuses. This work tries to apply well-known scheduling theories and previous work in the field of response time analysis for PROFIBUS messages in the analysis and simulation of the overall distributed system. The first step was to get together previous studies. After that, a tool called BERTA (Basic Environment for Real Time Analysis) was designed in order to embody deduced algorithms for schedulability analysis as well as simulation of the distributed system.
div.p: BERTA is presented here in its veyfirst version.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A Real Time System is [2] any system which has to respond to extemally generated stimuli within a jhite and specified delay. Thus, Embedded or Real Time Systems usually have to meet hard requirements in terms of response time, performance and security. They can be found in diverse fields such as aerospace, railway traffic control, automation, etc. Sometimes, not the whole system, but a subset of actions has to meet this kind of requirements. As they have specific requirements that differ from requirements in common computer based systems, particular analysis must be performed to assure they meet specifications.

Many studies have been focused on defining scheduling methods in order to analyze the temporal behaviour of processes involved in a real time system. The aim is to guarantee deadlines for every critical task A. F. L6pez University of the Basque Country(UPV/EHU) Alameda de Urquijo s/n 480 13 Bilbao (Spain) jtplovaf @bi.ehu.es in the system. Most of them use static priority preemptive schedulers, which assure the execution of the task (in executable status) with the highest priority in every moment. Liu and Layland [8] show how a set of tasks can have guaranteed deadlines if the priority assignment policy is rate monotonic (highest priority is assigned to the task with the lowest period). Moreover, the Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) method is proposed, which allows to check that a set of tasks will be executed before their deadlines finish. In the particular case of tasks with deadlines equal to periods, the Rate Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) is an optimal way of dealing with priorities because if deadlines can not be guaranteed in this way, no other static scheduling policy can guarantee them.

Even imposing serious restrictions on involved tasks (tasks must be periodical and independent, deadlines equal to periods and there must be no blocking by external events), the work of Liu and Layland was an starting point for many researchers who have extended the defined model for tasks to a wide range of applications. In this way, Joseph and Panya [7] completed the model and enabled the analysis of tasks with deadline lower than period. They proved that the Deadline Monotonic Scheduling (DMS) is optimal in this case because if deadlines are not met, no other static priority policy will guarantee them.

Lehoczky et a1 [9] proposed Event Servers in order to qualify RMA to handle sporadic tasks. Rajkumar et a1 [ 181 extend DMA allowing external blocking. Sha et a1 [ 191 overcome the inter-task communication restriction and proposed the use of Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) to set bounds to the blocking time a task can suffer due to others with lower priority. The Blocking Factor (B), which represents the worst-case time a task can be blocked due to the operation of the priority ceiling protocol (or equivalent concurrency control protocol), must be added to the response time of that task. Bi (blocking factor for task i) is normally equal to the longest critical section of lower priority tasks accessing semaphores with ceilings higher than (or equal to) the priority of i. Tindell at a1 [21] define a release jitter (the scheduler mechanism takes a bounded time to recognize the arrival of a task and it is wrong the assumption that a task is always released as soon as it arrives), establish a suflcient and necessary test of schedulability, describe how the schedulability analysis can be updated to determine worst-case response times when tasks can behave as sporadically periodic tasks (executing with an inner period ti and outer period ) and derive analysis that permits tasks to have arbitrary deadlines.

Usually, a distributed system involves a set of processors, sensors and actuators connected through a network. In a system like this, every action should have a bounded response time, not only tasks executing concurrently in each processor, but also messages that share the network. The worst case response time should be known in advance for every operation, in order to ensure that local and end-to-end deadlines will be satisfied.

The temporal demands mentioned above gave rise to the specification of fieldbuses. The main feature of these so called real time networks is the fact of having a deterministic temporal behaviour. During the past decade several commercial solutions have been proposed for this type of applications. For example FIP Vasques [23], [24], [25]) have studied these communication protocols and it has been proved that it is feasible to compute the response time for a set of messages, in the worst case of the system temporal behaviour. A unified temporal analysis for tasks in processors and messages in the CAN network is presented by Burns et a1 [ 11. In this approach, and due to the inherent characteristics of this fieldbus, correspondences between messages and tasks lead to the use of similar analysis methods to schedule them. In this sense, this work aims to build a flexible and extensible tool that gathers up mentioned studies. This tool should perform the temporal analysis and simulation, in a particular scenario, for an specified distributed system and it should be helpful to guarantee, from the very first phases in the design, the fulfil of real time requirements. There is a current version of BERTA that performs analysis and simulation for distributed systems over CAN bus (Marcos et a1 [lo], [ 111). This paper focuses on the design of BERTA over PROFIBUS.

The layout of the paper is as follows: In section 2 previous work in PROFIBUS temporal behaviour is briefly commented. Section 3 describes the temporal model of the distributed system used in BERTA as well as the temporal equations that apply for both tasks and messages involved in the distributed system. These equations allow the computation of the worst case response times. In section 4 specifications for BERTA as well as the design are described. Section 5 presents a case study and the paper finishes with some conclusions and future work.

div.p: Let us assume a distributed system consisting of a set of tasks (qj) mapped into i nodes (j tasks in each node) and a set of messages that communicate some of those tasks. div.head: Specifications for BERTA
div.p: The iterative method used to compute every response time within a distributed system needs a software tool that embodies every computation. Further on, simulation of other scenarios different to the worst case would be interesting in order to analyze other temporal behaviour than the worst case, detect deadlocks, foresee common situations, etc. BERTA (Basic Environment for Real-Time Analysis) is a tool that owns these features, worst case analysis and any-case simulation, and it offers graphical interface for model editing and analyzing simulation results. Although it is a complete tool by itself, it will be integrated with other tools in a more general environment called RTF: Real Time Framework (Marcos et a1 [l 11, [12]). This framework would help along the specification, analysis, design, simulation and implementation phases in the building of distributed systems with real time requirements. In this sense, interfaces with those tools should be considered because data will have to flow fiom one application to other assuring information consistency.
Specifications for BERTA can be summarized in the following:

-Ability to modifL or extend the model parameters and complete the temporal analysis (with other scheduling policies, communication networks, access protocol to shared resources, ...) -User friendly graphical interface from which a model file will be created or edited.
-Graphical output for temporal simulation.

-Standard format for input data to BERTA and for the analysis results. As input data could be obtained &om other tool in RTF and also results could be used by others, a well-defined data format will make easy the reuse of data.

div.head: Design of BERTA
div.p: MATLAB (Mathworks [13]) has been selected as simulation environment and programming language in order to build BERTA. It has been proved to be a flexible and simple way to handle issues fiom diverse knowledge fields. This is important in RTF because in the whole development of a distributed real time system it is necessary to integrate control and computer science issues. Main characteristics of Matlab include:

-Power of computation -Easy programming of iterative algorithms -Easy handle of data structures -Graphical facilities to build user interface -Simulation ability BERTA performs its analysis and simulation over a temporal model of the distributed system. This model reflects only those parameters relevant for analyzing temporal behaviour. This information is organized in objects (entities): processors, networks, messages, tasks, events and resources. The relationship between these objects is represented in the figure 2. The graphical interface allows the user to specify the temporal model of the distributed system. This interface module generates an ASCII file written following a context-free grammar (Hopcroft and Ullman [5]). After BERTA computes this input file, results (simulation or analysis results) are stored in the output ASCII file, using the same notation, and the output interface module offers a graphical view of the results. Thus, ASCII files make easy the integration of every module in BERTA and the integration with other tools inside RTF.

The definition of the context-free grammar makes easier the control of syntactical mistakes. Figure 3 shows the grammar elements and their parameters. They represent the different entities that can be part of a distributed system: processor, network, task, message and event. This grammar can be extended as BERTA grows not only introducing new entities but also augmenting the parameters of a particular entity. The graphical interface (written in JAVA) has been designed in order to dynamically accept definitions of new elements. -File reading: This module processes every information in the input file, reports syntactical mistakes and stores values in variables used by the temporal analysis.
-Temporal analysis: The worst case response time is computed for every task.
-Simulation: Any situation described by user is simulated.
-Graphical interface: It performs interaction with user allowing model edition, graphical output of results.

div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: A flexible tool that embodies current temporal studies has been presented. It incorporates easy integration of other scheduling policies, protocols for access to shared resources and a good way to compare the efficiency of different temporal studies. The design enforces integration with other tools through an ASCII file interface. A context-free grammar is used to define model entities for the temporal model of a distributed system. A user-friendly graphical interface developed in JAVA allows the dynamic definition of new entities as well as extension of entity's temporal parameters.

Current work is focused in the use of Java for local or remote access to the tool and also in avoiding Matlabdependence by means of generating stand-alone executable file. Future goals include the introduction of more scheduling methods and other fieldbuses to allow comparison of their efficiency in order to select the most suitable for each case. Another goal is the inclusion of new advances in temporal studies and a better temporal model that relaxes current restrictions.
